hooks.text: Jupiter's famous storm plunges 200 miles deep into its atmosphere.
How deep does Jupiter's famous Great Red Spot actually go?
Jupiter's Great Red Spot isn't a cloud, but a deep canyon.

title: Jupiter's Storm is 200 Miles DEEP
description: Jupiter's iconic Great Red Spot isn't just a surface cloud. NASA's Juno mission reveals the storm plunges over 200 miles into the planet's atmosphere.

beats.text: Jupiter's famous storm plunges 200 miles deep into its atmosphere.
beats.visual: Juno spacecraft high-altitude view of the Great Red Spot, 2019

beats.text: Most people think it's just a thin, swirling surface cloud.
beats.visual: Hubble view of Jupiter's clouds and Great Red Spot, 2019

beats.text: But NASA's Juno spacecraft recently measured the giant planet's gravity.
beats.visual: Illustration of Juno spacecraft performing a close flyby of Jupiter, 2019

beats.text: It revealed a vertical vortex twice as deep as Earth's oceans.
beats.visual: 3D visualization of the Great Red Spot vertical structure, NASA, 2021

beats.text: The storm's roots reach far past where sunlight can even penetrate.
beats.visual: Artist rendering of Jupiter's deep, dark atmospheric layers, 2019

beats.text: Unlike Earth, Jupiter has no solid surface to create friction.
beats.visual: Global map of Jupiter's turbulent cloud belts, Juno, 2019

beats.text: This lack of resistance is why the storm plunges 200 miles deep.
beats.visual: Close-up of the turbulent center of the Great Red Spot, 2019

better_than_last: I applied the reviewer's specific wording for the vertical vortex and the friction comparison to ensure a tight loop and clear myth-busting structure.
